scenes.headline: How MotionBricks writes the motion between poses
scenes.sub: Three networks that serve characters and humanoid robots
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Mortar! This is a motion generator. Give it where a body has been and where it should go, and it writes the movement in between.

scenes.text: Predict the length and the root path first, then a few small codes for every four frames, and decode them into motion.
scenes.mark: a few small codes for every four frames
scenes.say: First the length and the path of the root. Then a few small codes for every four frames. Then a decoder turns them into motion.

steps.say: You supply four recent poses and up to four target poses.
The root predictor reads them and picks how long the clip is, and where the pelvis travels.
The pose predictor then chooses the motion codes, conditioned on that path and on your pinned poses.
The decoder turns codes and path into frames. Every token covers four frames, at thirty a second.
Each of up to sixteen positions starts as masked codes, plus the root path and any pinned pose.
Sixteen plain transformer layers read all positions at once.
One pass, and the best code in every head is taken. No sampling, so the same inputs give the same clip.

scenes.label: of pose weights read on every pass
scenes.note: so six positions cost about what sixteen do
scenes.say: Why is it cheap? Five hundred megabytes of weights are read every pass, so a short clip costs about what a long one does.

scenes.label: of each G1 token's capacity are used
scenes.say: Each token is eight small codes. By the stored counts, the tokenizer uses most of what those codes can carry.

scenes.text: One pass with no sampling means the same inputs give the same clip, so test it like a function.
scenes.mark: the same inputs give the same clip
scenes.say: One pass and no sampling. The same inputs give the same clip, so you can test it like a function.
Root first, then codes in one pass. It makes motion, and a controller still has to move the robot.
